It is a fairly safe assumption to make that during the course of their lives, each and every single person who lives in the United States of America will need the help, advice or representation in one shape or form of an attorney, whether it is a criminal, civil, divorce, business or contract lawyer any other type.

America’s extremely litigious society almost guarantees that this will happen.

Another fact worth mentioning is the often ridiculously high attorney fees that people are often force to pay whenever they need the services of a lawyer. This is the same for individuals as it is for businesses.

If the above statement is anything to go by, the question to ask yourself is what can you do to ensure that you find that lawyer who is not just out to get his or her next pay cheque, but is rather genuinely interested in ensuring that you obtain a favurable outcome with regards the situation you are facing, for which you need legal representation or advice? In this article, we offer 5 very useful things to consider before you agree to take on the services of any lawyer. It doesn’t matter what type of lawyer or what their specialty is, if you follow these tips, then you likely will reduce the chance of hiring someone who will not offer you the best possible representation that you need.

In no particular order of preference, we present our list.

  1. The Nature of Their Law Practice and Their Specialty: You most certainly want to know what branch of the law they specialize in. It is common practice for many lawyers and law firms to be multi-disciplined, but that doesn’t mean they are specialists in all these fields. Just as a General Practice doctor can never be a specialist in a field for which he is not trained in, and even a specialist in one field does not necessarily qualify him or her to be a specialist in a completely different field.

So be sure to find out what the attorney’s specialty is. How many years they have been practicing in that specialty, and several other related questions. The main objective here is to ascertain their possible level of knowledge and experience with handling matters that are related and relevant to the case for which you need them.

  1. Is There Any Conflict of Interest. The last thing you want is for someone to represent you in a legal case who also has a close relationship with your opponent. While in principle there is a such as thing separation of private and professional life or attorney client privilege, in reality who is to say that your opponent will not try to take advantage of any existing or even past relationship with your attorney, should one exist, to try and undermine your case?

Which is exactly why you need to know if the attorney you are considering hiring has had any dealings with the other party in the legal case you have, and what the nature of that relationship is or was. Whether it is a business or personal relationship is irrelevant. It is still in your best interest to know this fact.

  1. How Many Cases of a Similar Nature Have they Handled. You don’t want to hire an attorney who has very limited experience in dealing with situations that are similar in nature to yours.

There is a popular saying that practice makes for perfection. So chances are high that if the lawyer you are considering hiring has limited experience with cases of a similar nature to yours, they possibly might not be able to get you the best possible outcome.

So rather be safe than sorry and be sure to ask them what cases that are similar to yours that they have handled and just as importantly, ask about the outcome of those cases. Where possibly, independently verify what they tell you. Because lawyers have often been known to lie.

Bottom line is that you want someone akin to a specialist to handle your case.

However, I admit that this situation might be tricky. This is perhaps the exact same situation that young unemployed people face when looking for a job and all the jobs they see require that they have experience, but yet no employer will allow these individuals gain that experience by hiring them. Many (young) lawyers with no experience in a particular field might also face this dilemma, and in the same way I am an advocate for giving young inexperienced and unemployed people the chance to show what they can do, I am also in favor of giving inexperienced lawyers a chance to represent you despite not having vast experiences in cases of a similar nature.

The middle ground I would perhaps seek is to find out if the lawyer in question has ever worked under or shadowed a more experienced attorney, and this would go a long way on giving them second hand experience, which is often good enough.

  1. Knowledge of the Opposing Counsel. Another very important thing you want to know about any attorney you are thinking about hiring is what knowledge they might have of the opposing counsel. You want to know if the lawyer you are speaking to has ever been on the opposing side of the lawyers to the other party to your dispute and if so how many times. As well as the outcome of those cases. You will also want to know if your intended legal representative or team has ever lost to the legal representative of the other party to your issue, and if so how many times. In the same vein, you will also want to know if they have ever won a case against them, and if so how many times. The latter if is something that might boost your confidence in this lawyer.

  2. An Idea of What it will Cost: And by how much it will cost, I do not only refer to the legal or consultation fees you will pay to the lawyer. But rather what if the case goes to court? What if you will be needing a Private Investigator, and possibly a whole bunch of other things you may not have foreseen, or that you hoped it would not come to, but it does? You should always be prepared for the worst and hoping for the best, and the very first thing in preparing for the worst is knowing what it will or may cost you. At least in this case, from a financial standpoint.

In closing, it doesn’t matter what type of lawyer you are looking for, whether it is a lawyer to help you draft a contract for an employee you are considering hiring, or a litigation attorney to help advice you on a business dispute, to settle a family dispute or any other business dealings for which you need the service and advice of a lawyer, and irrespective of what city you are looking in, or in fact any state in the country, these above 5 things are very and critically important things you need to know, as a minimum.

What is it like to be in the hospital for alcohol detox?

Been in the hospital for withdrawals multiple times. Depends on how bad the withdrawals are. Withdrawals are hell, shakes all through your body, feels like your brain is being ripped to pieces, fever, sweats, and possibly seizures and hallucinations. If your friend has had a seizure or has been hallucinating he'll stay in the hospital to be monitored closely with IVs for Ativan or Valium (benzodiazepines) and saline to rehydrate him. Possibly staying up to week. If your friend doesn't absolutely need to be hospitalized then he'll be sent to a detox where they'll still put him on a regiment of benzos for 72 hours. Hospitals are much more empathic towards the withdrawal symptoms and if you show any sign of shakes or whatever you'll get another dose to calm back down. In detox depending on how bad it is there are set times when you can have your dose, your friend might just have to shake it out for a few days. Detoxs are nasty places, at least in my experience, the food is from the county jail, half the people literally live there or the homeless shelter. Smells awful in your shared room with 3-5 other people. After they're out tell your friend you're concerned and maybe he should think about treatment. There's millions of people out there who suffer from addiction but there's a lot of help too. Best of wishes to your friend. I wouldn't wish withdrawals on anyone.
